name: Chemical-resistant gloves (butyl, neoprene, nitrile, Viton, laminate)
summary: Thicker reusable gloves made to keep a liquid chemical off your skin for a set time, but only the chemicals their material resists.
uses: Only as good as the match: no material resists every chemical or any chemical forever; look it up in the maker's chart (HSE GLOVES, ANSELL CRG)
Butyl: acetone, MEK, esters, concentrated sulfuric and hydrofluoric acid. Weak against petrol, toluene, xylene and chlorinated solvents (OSHA 3151, ANSELL CRG)
Thick nitrile: petrol, kerosene, oils, alcohols and caustic. Not for acetone, MEK, dichloromethane, concentrated sulfuric or 70% nitric acid (ANSELL CRG, OSHA 3151)
Neoprene: many acids, caustics and alcohols, but only 24 minutes against concentrated sulfuric acid; not recommended for toluene, xylene or chlorinated solvents (ANSELL CRG)
Viton and laminate films suit aromatic and chlorinated solvents, yet lasted only 20 to 30 minutes against dichloromethane. PVA resists solvents but water ruins it (ANSELL CRG, VT EHS GLOVES)
Trichloroethylene: OSHA 3151 says nitrile protects, Ansell rates its thick nitrile not recommended. Treat nitrile as unsuitable unless the maker's chart says otherwise (OSHA 3151, ANSELL CRG)
identify: Thicker than disposables and often gauntlet length: the gloves in Ansell's tests were 0.30 to 0.68 mm (12 to 27 mil), and its laminate film glove only 0.06 mm (ANSELL CRG). Find the maker, material and model on the glove, bag or box; chart ratings belong to that exact product (ANSELL CRG, HSE GLOVES). European mark: EN ISO 374-1 flask with Type A (over 30 minutes against at least 6 test chemicals), Type B (over 30 minutes, 3 chemicals) or Type C (over 10 minutes, 1 chemical), plus letters: A methanol, B acetone, C acetonitrile, D dichloromethane, E carbon disulphide, F toluene, G diethylamine, H tetrahydrofuran, I ethyl acetate, J heptane, K 40% caustic soda, L 96% sulfuric acid, M 65% nitric acid, N acetic acid, O 25% ammonia, P 30% peroxide, S 40% hydrofluoric acid, T 37% formaldehyde. Levels 1 to 6 mean over 10, 30, 60, 120, 240 and 480 minutes (EJENDALS EN 374). On older gloves EN 374-3 means chemical protection; EN 374-2 alone means only waterproof (HSE GLOVES). With no chemical mark, the maker's chart decides; for pesticides, the label says whether gloves are needed; the maker can say which (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES). Waterproof is not the same as chemical-resistant (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES).
test: Before each use, look and feel: reject gloves that are stained, softened, swollen, sticky, stiff, cracked, dissolving or leaking (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES, HSE GLOVES). Pinholes: swing the glove to trap air inside, then squeeze it so any leak shows (CCOHS GLOVES), or pour water in and watch for drips (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES). Breakthrough is the chemical reaching the inside; degradation is the glove itself swelling, hardening or softening, and either can ruin it. A glove can be permeated and still look unchanged (HSE GLOVES, ANSELL CRG), so a used glove of unknown history is suspect. Fit: cover all skin with no gap at the sleeve (CCOHS GLOVES); cuffs folded or over the sleeve when working overhead, sleeves over the gloves when working down (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES). Chart times are for the pure chemical in a lab; for a mixture, go by the part with the shortest breakthrough, though only testing the mixture is certain (HSE GLOVES). If chemical gets inside, take them off, wash your hands and change gloves (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES). After use, wash the outside with detergent and running water before taking them off, then hang them to dry; don't soak them (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES).

decay.note: Nitrile, neoprene and PVC have a nominal 5-year shelf life and natural latex about 3; heat, sunlight and ozone shorten it, and used gloves may already be permeated (S+H SHELF LIFE, ANSELL CRG).

improvise: First avoid contact: pour with a funnel, use tongs or a long-handled scoop, and work upwind with water ready to rinse. Thin nitrile disposables are splash protection only: change at once after a splash, and expect acetone, methanol, xylene or dichloromethane to get through in about a minute (KC NITRILE). Household latex rubber gloves may resist most water solutions of acids, alkalis and salts (OSHA 3151), but Ansell rates natural rubber not recommended for concentrated sulfuric acid and 70% nitric acid, and it is poor against solvents, oils and fuels (ANSELL CRG, VT EHS GLOVES). A waterproof glove is not automatically chemical-resistant (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES). Plastic bags tear and their resistance is unknown: not protection. Useless: leather and cloth gloves soak chemicals up and hold them on your skin (HC PESTICIDE GLOVES). For hydrofluoric acid, strong solvents or anything that says fatal in contact with skin, don't work without a glove whose chart or EN 374 mark covers it (letter S is 40% hydrofluoric acid); leave it (ANSELL CRG, EJENDALS EN 374). If you are splashed, take the glove off and wash the skin with lots of water at once.
